extracted.intended_audience: recipients of Federal financial assistance (elementary/secondary schools, postsecondary institutions, libraries, museums), Title IX coordinators, campus administrators, legal/compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing when and how a recipient may undertake an emergency removal of a respondent under §106.44(c) of the Title IX regulations, including required analyses, due process features, interactions with disability and other laws, and permissible scope of actions during and after removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency removal justification: immediate threat to physical health or safety arising from allegations of sexual harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(c) permits removal when an individualized safety and risk analysis determines the respondent poses an immediate threat to the physical health or safety of any student or other individual, and that threat arises from the allegations of sexual harassment as defined in §106.30.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include threats of physical violence against a complainant in response to allegations or a respondent threatening self-harm in reaction to allegations. The Department revised the provision to require the threat be to the 'physical' health or safety and to arise 'from the allegations of sexual harassment' to limit emergency removal to genuine physical emergencies tied to Title IX allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualized safety and risk analysis is required before emergency removal
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must first undertake an individualized safety and risk analysis that determines an immediate threat to physical health or safety justifies removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to prescribe detailed methodological requirements (e.g., objective evidence, current medical knowledge, licensed evaluator) so recipients retain flexibility. The analysis need not be performed for every reported sexual assault; it is required only when considering an emergency removal. Recipients may adopt more prescriptive practices if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of protected persons: 'any student or other individual' (single-person threats permitted)
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation replaces 'students or employees' with 'any student or other individual' to clarify emergency removals may be based on threats to a single person as well as multiple persons, and may include the respondent themself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This revision ensures emergency removal can address threats to one individual (complainant, respondent, or another person) rather than being limited to multiple persons or employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on physical (not solely mental/emotional) health or safety
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule adds the word 'physical' to 'health or safety' to ensure the emergency removal provision applies to bona fide physical health or safety emergencies rather than to mental or emotional well-being alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional or mental harms are intended to be addressed by supportive measures rather than by emergency removal under §106.44(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency removal is not a substitute for the §106.45 grievance process
rubrics_metrics.description: Emergency removal addresses immediate risks to physical health or safety and does not substitute for reaching a determination as to the respondent's responsibility for sexual harassment under §106.45.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary sanctions (suspension, expulsion, etc.) that punish respondents for responsibility must follow the §106.45 grievance process; emergency removal is a temporary measure to address imminent threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and opportunity to challenge: post-deprivation process sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients need only provide the basic features of due process (notice and opportunity to be heard), and may provide that opportunity after removal rather than before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to require a 'full hearing' pre-deprivation; post-removal challenge rights must exist. Separately, §106.45 grievance proceedings have their own live-hearing requirements for adjudication of responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients have discretion over scope and conditions of removal when threshold met
rubrics_metrics.description: If the high threshold for emergency removal is met (individualized analysis shows immediate physical threat), the recipient may determine the appropriate scope and conditions of removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to require removals be 'narrowly tailored' beyond the requirement that the threat 'justifies' removal, allowing recipients flexibility to address particular emergency circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may rely on objective evidence or licensed evaluators but are not required to
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to mandate that risk assessments be based on objective evidence, current medical knowledge, or a licensed evaluator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may adopt such prescriptive requirements in their own policies, but the Title IX regulation intentionally leaves flexibility so recipients can tailor emergency responses to their contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency removal applies only where the threat arises from sexual harassment allegations under §106.30
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation clarifies that the justification for emergency removal must 'arise from the allegations of sexual harassment' so §106.44(c) governs only emergencies tied to Title IX sexual harassment allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threats or illegal conduct that do not arise from sexual harassment allegations should be addressed under the recipient's code of conduct, other laws, or other policies, not §106.44(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must comply with disability laws (IDEA, Section 504, ADA) when conducting removals
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(c) acknowledges recipients may have obligations under the IDEA, Section 504, and the ADA that affect how emergency removals are conducted and states that the provision does not modify those rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, under IDEA a school may need an IEP-team process before removing a student receiving special education, and recipients should involve disability services as appropriate. The regulations do not relieve recipients from complying with state or federal disability obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special education procedural constraints may limit unilateral removals
rubrics_metrics.description: In elementary/secondary settings, IDEA protections may constrain unilateral administrator removals where conduct is a manifestation of a disability; placement decisions may require the involvement of the IEP team and parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must follow IDEA procedures where applicable; emergency removal under Title IX cannot override IDEA-mandated processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of bias and requirement for impartiality in removal proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must ensure emergency removal proceedings are impartial and free from bias or conflicts of interest, including avoiding implicit bias against students with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes recipients may provide training to Title IX personnel about obligations under Title IX and applicable disability laws to prevent biased decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures should be offered and recipients may mitigate academic harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients are required to offer supportive measures to every complainant; commenters urged and the Department recognized that recipients often should provide alternative academic accommodations to respondents removed on an emergency basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While §106.44(c) does not require specific accommodations (e.g., alternative access to classes, re-taking missed exams), recipients often develop 'safe exit plans' and may choose to secure property or provide academic continuity. Failure to take such steps is not automatically Title IX discrimination unless applied discriminatorily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department declines to require periodic review of emergency removal decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule does not require recipients to periodically review emergency removals; the Department concluded post-deprivation opportunity to challenge and the prompt time frames in §106.45 suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients retain discretion over procedures for review; the Department chose not to add mandatory review layers that could complicate emergency responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement in §106.44(c) to notify authorities, provide safety interventions, or publicly report removals
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to state in §106.44(c) that recipients must comply with the Clery Act, notify law enforcement, provide specified safety interventions, or publicly report the annual number of emergency removals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may still be required to take such actions under other laws or institutional policies; §106.44(c) neither imposes nor precludes those steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency removal may occur even when no grievance process has been initiated
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may undertake an emergency removal in situations where an immediate threat exists before an investigation or grievance process under §106.45 is underway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to forbid emergency removals until the conclusion of a grievance process, finding such a restriction could impair prompt responses to genuine emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and local law considerations must be heeded but regulations govern in conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients should follow additional relevant standards imposed by state or local law when conducting emergency removals, but where there is a direct conflict the Title IX final regulations prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should strive to reconcile requirements to the greatest extent possible and seek technical assistance as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstruction of investigation or risk of destroying evidence does not, by itself, justify emergency removal under §106.44(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department disagreed that a recipient's assessment that a respondent might obstruct an investigation or destroy evidence alone is sufficient to justify an emergency removal under §106.44(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §106.44(c) is intended to address health or safety emergencies arising from sexual harassment allegations, not all forms of misconduct during a grievance process; other recipient codes or laws may address obstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential mitigation for respondents later found not responsible is discretionary, not required
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters requested mandatory remediation (e.g., retaking classes, restoring property) for respondents removed and later found not responsible; the Department did not adopt a requirement to mandate mitigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may choose to mitigate harms (allow re-taking classes, secure property, provide academic accommodations) but §106.44(c) does not compel such remedies; however, state law or contracts might provide additional remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency removal can encompass threats to respondent's own physical safety (self-harm)
rubrics_metrics.description: By referencing the physical health or safety 'of any student or other individual,' §106.44(c) includes situations where a respondent's threat of self-harm, arising from sexual harassment allegations, may justify removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This alignment with FERPA's health or safety exception allows recipients to consider imminent risks to the respondent themself when those risks arise from the Title IX allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations under §106.44(a): non-deliberately indifferent response and documentation if supportive measures are not provided
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient is obligated under §106.44(a) to provide a complainant with a non-deliberately indifferent response, including offering supportive measures designed to protect the complainant's safety; if supportive measures are not provided, the recipient must document reasons under §106.45(b)(10)(ii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergency removal remains an option when an individualized safety and risk analysis supports it, but recipients must still satisfy their broader duties to offer and document supportive measures.
